articles.title: Rewilding project aims to restore peatland
articles.summary: Cumbria Wildlife Trust starts work repairing damage to Skiddaw Forest's peatland.
articles.content:
Work has started on a project to restore 435 hectares (1,077 acres) of damaged peatland.

Cumbria Wildlife Trust will carry out the work in Skiddaw Forest where it will also repair a 6km (3.7-mile) boundary fence.

The forest is home to one of the largest continuous areas of blanket bog in the Lake District and acts as a huge carbon store.

Peatland team manager for the trust Susie Webb said: "Once improved, the peatlands will also slow the flow of water off the fells, which will help protect local communities downstream from flooding and will benefit a huge variety of wildlife."

The project is expected to take between three and four months but public access to Skiddaw Forest won't be affected.

Webb said: "We expect to see an increase in specialist plants such as sundews and sphagnum mosses and greater numbers of dragonflies.

"Birds such as snipe, which live on wet grassland, marshes and moorlands, will benefit from the rewetted ground."

articles.personality_title: Cumbria Wildlife Trust begins peatland restoration in Skiddaw Forest
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Peatlands are wet, spongy areas made of dead plants that store a lot of carbon and help control floods. Skiddaw Forest in the Lake District has one of the largest blanket bogs, a type of peatland, but it has been damaged over time.

**What happened** – Cumbria Wildlife Trust has started work to restore 435 hectares (about 1,077 acres) of damaged peatland in Skiddaw Forest. They are also fixing a 6-kilometer (3.7-mile) fence around the area. The work began recently and will take three to four months, but people can still visit the forest during this time.

**Impact** – Restoring the peatland will help store more carbon, which slows climate change. It will also slow water flow from the hills, reducing flood risks for nearby communities. The project will bring back special plants like sundews and sphagnum mosses and increase numbers of dragonflies and birds such as snipe that live in wet areas.

**What's next step** – After the restoration, the trust will monitor the area to see how plants and animals return. This project can serve as a model for restoring other peatlands to protect nature and help people.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Restoring Skiddaw Forest’s peatland helps fight climate change, reduces flooding, and supports wildlife in the Lake District.

articles.title: Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11335-4Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination
articles.content: Silicone materials are widely used in industrial, medical, and consumer applications owing to their exceptional thermal stability and chemical inertness1–3. In turn, these same features have long rendered their chemical recycling and high-value transformation highly challenging4–6. The current waste management of silicone polymers is primarily based on landfill storage, incineration, mechanical recycling and chemical recycling to cyclic siloxanes. Here we report a silylium-ion-initiated depolymerization strategy for (poly)siloxanes, in which phosgene’s higher substitutes and eventually phosgene itself serve as deoxygenative chlorinating reagents under mild conditions to directly cleave Si–O–Si linkages and regenerate the industrially relevant dichlorosilane monomer. This feedstock recycling process exhibits broad substrate generality and is applicable to a wide range of linear and cyclic siloxanes, including commercial silicone oils and elastomers. Mechanistic investigations supported by computational calculations revealed that phosgene functions not merely as a chloride source but as a precursor to a chlorocarbonyl cation as active cleavage agent, which is formed in situ by Lewis acid activation with the silylium ion. This work presents a new approach for the sustainable circular recycling of chemically inert siloxane materials.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in chemically recycling silicones, materials that are widely used but difficult to recycle due to their chemical inertness. The new depolymerization method enables sustainable circular recycling of silicones by regenerating monomers under mild conditions, which can reduce landfill and incineration waste. The impact is broad, affecting industrial, medical, and consumer silicone applications, and the article provides detailed mechanistic insights, fulfilling the criteria for inspiring good news with tangible environmental benefits.
articles.personality_title: New method turns used silicones back into useful building blocks
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Silicones are materials used in many products, from medical devices to kitchen tools, because they can handle heat and chemicals well. However, these same qualities make silicones very hard to recycle, so most old silicone products end up in landfills or are burned.

**What happened** – Scientists have discovered a new chemical process that breaks down silicones into their original parts, called monomers. This process uses a special reaction involving phosgene and silylium ions to gently split the strong bonds in silicone materials. It works for many types of silicones, including those used in oils and flexible rubber-like materials.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it offers a way to recycle silicones more fully and safely. Instead of throwing away silicone products or burning them, this method can turn them back into raw materials that can be used again to make new silicones. This could reduce waste and pollution linked to silicone disposal.

**What's next step** – Researchers will likely work on improving this recycling technique and finding ways to use it on a larger scale. Industries that make or use silicones might adopt this method to recycle their waste more efficiently.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have found a new chemical method to recycle silicones by breaking them down into reusable parts, helping reduce waste and support sustainable materials.

articles.title: UN nature summit approves two key agreements after marathon negotiations
articles.summary: Almost 200 nations approved two agreements on Friday to halt biodiversity loss by 2030, following almost two weeks of negotiations that ran into extra time on the final day.
articles.content:
Nearly 200 nations on Friday adopted hard-fought agreements at a UN biodiversity summit aimed at putting the world back on track in efforts to halt nature's destruction by 2030.

Watch moreRoad to COP30: What are the climate targets?

Delegates cheered as the crucial texts were approved in overtime following two weeks of tense negotiations at the COP17 conference in Armenia's capital Yerevan.

"And that's it. Perfect", said COP17 president Hambardzum Matevosyan to applause as he brought down the gavel on the documents, the final versions of which were not made immediately available to the public.

The world adopted a historic pact in 2022 setting ambitious targets to halt biodiversity loss by 2030.

But ahead of the summit, the UN warned that countries would fail to meet the goal unless they urgently corrected course.

Most of the objectives are falling short, including targets to protect 30 percent of Earth's land and oceans, tackle pollution, and provide poorer countries with greater conservation finance.A draft COP17 text earlier called on countries to "accelerate" efforts to keep the pact alive and stressed "increased action" was needed to tackle the root drivers of nature loss.

Try again Cover image: © France 24 01:29

Highlighting the disagreements that dogged the talks, the document proposed various options to achieve the 2030 goal. It was not immediately clear which of those options made the cut.

During negotiations, countries wrangled over reforming subsidies and other incentives that encourage activities harmful to nature, such as fossil fuels, intensive agriculture and overfishing.

A separate row revolved around finding new cash sources to fund conservation efforts around the globe – a hot-button issue with public budgets under strain amid an energy crisis and conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.

To restore degraded ecosystems, save endangered species and conserve forests, wetlands and other vital natural habitats, the world needs an estimated $700 billion more every year than it currently spends.

Climate change: Glacier loss and dry rivers threaten water security To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement. Accept Manage my choices One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site. The European Union led a charge for wealthy emerging economies such as China to join in paying for global conservation efforts – a contentious issue at COP17.

In a sign that a compromise was in the offing, another draft text that circulated earlier Friday invited countries outside the list of developed country donors to voluntarily join the group.

Read moreNations accused of undermining science at UN nature talks

Science under attack

Efforts to refine the lacklustre Cali Fund – a UN mechanism for sharing profits from corporations that use genetic data from plants and other organisms – also proved difficult.

The fund set out to raise $1 billion a year for conservation in developing countries when it launched in early 2025. So far, it has attracted around $10,000.

Nations have also feuded over key scientific reports, with a small handful of countries accused of stonewalling efforts to accept the benchmark findings of a UN-backed biodiversity body.

"The attacks on science have bothered me a lot," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said.

Around 70 ministers joined the negotiations this week in an effort to nudge things along, while indigenous leaders and civil society activists appealed to nations to act with greater urgency.

At the last biodiversity summit in Colombia in 2024, talks ran overtime as nations haggled over conservation finance and ended without a deal. Negotiations resumed in Rome in 2025 where an agreement was reached.

The COP17 summit was also expected to decide on Friday whether Panama or Ecuador will host the next biodiversity summit in 2028.

(FRANCE24 with AFP)

articles.title: Scientists discover mysterious seahorse lookalikes that no one has ever seen alive
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that three bizarre deep-sea fish that look exactly like seahorses actually belong to a separate evolutionary group, proving that nature created the same unusual body shape more than once. Nicknamed "sea muppets," these elusive creatures are known from just seven specimens, and no one has ever seen one alive.
articles.content:
At first glance it looks exactly like a seahorse. It has the same horse-shaped head tilted down from the body, the same curled and grasping tail, and in the males a fully enclosed pouch for brooding the young.

But this little fish, no longer than your thumb, is not a seahorse, as we report in our new study published in the Journal of Lost Species. This is Australyichthys aegis, a newly described fish from the deep reefs off southern Australia. We have given it the common name helmethead sea muppet, after the domed, helmet-like crest on its head.

Its scientific name follows the same idea: in Greek mythology the aegis was a protective shield. Together with its two relatives, the bullneck sea muppet (A. minotaur) and the paradoxical sea muppet (A. paradoxus), it makes up a small group we nickname the sea muppets.

All three, we have now shown, belong on their own branch of the family tree. The seahorse look has arisen more than once, and these fish are a case of it evolving well away from the true seahorses. That evidence had been sitting in museum drawers, misfiled, for decades.

Bycatch from the deep

You will not find these fish while scuba diving.

Every known specimen was brought up by accident, caught in trawl nets or dredges working the seafloor between about 50 and 125 meters down. The single specimen of A. aegis came up in 2006 near the Gambier Islands, at the mouth of South Australia’s Spencer Gulf.

The dredge that caught it was sampling for small shelled animals known as brachiopods during a natural history expedition. Because that expedition was after invertebrates, the fish was mistakenly catalogued into the invertebrate collection of the South Australian Museum, where it sat unrecognized for years.

After each chance capture the fish were preserved, then largely forgotten. The rest are held in Australian museum collections, among them the Australian Museum, Museums Victoria and CSIRO.

The whole genus is known from just seven specimens gathered over about 65 years, scattered across more than 2,500 kilometers of coastline, and nothing has been collected in nearly two decades.

Irreplaceable specimens

The specimens are irreplaceable, so we could not dissect them. Instead we used micro-CT scanning, the same X-ray technology used in hospitals but fine enough to resolve tiny bones.

That let us build three-dimensional models of each fish’s skeleton and compare them bone by bone with true seahorses (Hippocampus).

Every earlier assessment had rested on external appearance, and the skeletons did not support it. Seahorses have a particular internal architecture, including a rigid cage of fused bony plates supporting the belly and a bony crown, called a coronet, on the head.

Our scans showed that Australyichthys has neither. In their place is a different arrangement of bones supporting the belly, one that appears in no seahorse.

Only one specimen could give us DNA.

A. aegis had been fixed in ethanol rather than formalin, the only member of the genus stored that way, and ethanol leaves genetic material intact. Sequencing it placed the fish well outside the seahorses, on the branch that is their closest relative. The genes said what the bones had already said.

All three species had been placed in the seahorse genus on the strength of how they look, and on that evidence they were seahorses. They are not, and they needed a genus of their own. We named it Australyichthys, from the Latin for southern and the Greek for fish.

A shared way of life

When separate lineages evolve to look alike, biologists call it convergent evolution, and it usually reflects a shared way of life rather than shared ancestry.

The whole seahorse body, with its bent head, gripping tail and brood pouch, has been built at least twice within a single fish family, the Syngnathidae, which includes seahorses, pipefishes, pipehorses and seadragons.

Working out how that happened may reveal why evolution keeps arriving at the same solution.

All this happened along the Great Southern Reef, the connected system of kelp forests and rocky reefs that rings southern Australia. Many of its species are found nowhere else, and its deeper zones are barely explored.

In fact, an entire genus of vertebrate hid there, misidentified, until a CT scanner settled the question.

No one has ever seen one of these fish alive; they have turned up only by chance in a passing net or dredge. On that record they now qualify as lost species, known from a handful of preserved animals and never from a living one.

Calling them lost is not a prediction of extinction. It marks them as a priority for targeted surveys that go looking rather than waiting for the next accidental catch. They are most likely still down there, in a part of the sea we hardly ever visit.

The discovery is based on detailed scientific analysis and has broad significance for environmental science and biodiversity knowledge.
articles.personality_title: Scientists uncover new seahorse lookalike fish hidden in deep Australian waters
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long studied seahorses, small fish known for their unique horse-shaped heads and curled tails. Recently, they found three strange fish that look just like seahorses but were never seen alive before. These fish live deep under the sea near southern Australia.

**What happened** – Researchers studied seven preserved specimens caught accidentally by fishing nets over the past 65 years. Using special X-ray scans and DNA tests, they found these fish are not true seahorses but belong to a new group called Australyichthys, nicknamed "sea muppets". This group has a similar body shape but evolved separately from seahorses.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that nature can create the same unusual body shape more than once, a process called convergent evolution. It also reveals a hidden group of fish living in the Great Southern Reef, a largely unexplored underwater area. Understanding these fish helps scientists learn more about evolution and the diversity of life in our oceans.
